# Monolith fairness review

This review asks whether the baseline is a monolith a competent engineer would really build, or a strawman built to lose.

**Verdict.** The baseline is a working, reasonable first build. The differences it shows against the layered platform are architectural (where responsibilities live), not handicaps. The known asymmetries are listed at the end, together with the direction each one pushes the results.

## Held identical in both architectures

| Held identical | How |
|---|---|
| Scenario and data | The same `simulated_enterprise/data/inc4917.yaml`, with a fresh world database per scenario |
| Tools | The same MCP servers (`itsm`, `observability`, `deploy`), started the same way over stdio with the same SDK version |
| Model and options | `gpt-oss:20b`, `think: low`, temperature 0, `num_ctx` 16384, the same seed per scenario (model B: `qwen3:8b`, `think: false`) |
| Knowledge | The same runbook file, RB-CHK-007. The monolith inlines all of it; the layered platform retrieves sections of it |
| Memory | The same `memory_seed.yaml` entries for `checkout-api` |
| Task | The same user sentence; E6 uses the same adversarial sentence for both |
| Approval intent | Production changes (rollback, restart, scale) need approval in both. In both the approver is the simulated incident commander |
| Failure injection | The same fault, armed in the same world, applied inside the same MCP server; the same named crash moment |
| Record/replay | The same HTTP tape transport at the Ollama boundary. The same neutral ledgers (the world's executions, the tape's model calls) are scored by the same code |
| Scoring | `layered_platform/evals/checks.py` reads the world and the final report, never an architecture's belief about itself |

## What the monolith does well (deliberately)

- **Approval is enforced in code, not in the prompt.** `_execute_tool` asks the approver before any production rollback, restart or scale. E6 shows the planned production rollback gated in both architectures.
- **It never retries a write.** A timed-out write is reported to the model as an error. It is not retried blindly; the old F2 monolith did that, and it was a strawman.
- **It retries reads on timeout,** and retries model HTTP errors with backoff.
- **It keeps a session history on disk.** This uses the common chat-history semantics: a finished turn is appended when the run completes.
- **It writes a structured trace log** with timestamps, process ids, token counts and tool outcomes.
- **It is short and readable.** It is about 200 lines and ran INC-4917 correctly in the smoke tests, often faster and with fewer model calls per run than the layered platform.

## What the monolith does not have, and why that is not a handicap

These are the responsibilities the article argues need a home. Giving them to the monolith *is* building those layers:

| Missing | Consequence tested | Why it is not added to the baseline |
|---|---|---|
| An action identity (a deterministic key per side effect) | E4, E5 | The model can pass an idempotency key (the tool schema offers one), and in the recording it sometimes does. But nothing in the design owns a key that stays stable across retries and processes. Adding one means adding an operation store: the Tools + Actions layer |
| Durable per-step state | E5, E7 | Persisting progress after every step, and resuming from it, is the Agent Runtime layer |
| A policy that can deny, not just ask | E6 | An allow-list of "needs approval" tools is what a first build has. A default-deny registry is the Tools + Actions layer plus policy |
| A workflow identity in telemetry | E8 | It would need a workflow concept, which is the Orchestration layer |

## Known asymmetries

| Asymmetry | Which way it pushes the results |
|---|---|
| The monolith sends the whole runbook and all tools on every turn; the layered platform sends retrieved runbook sections and only read capabilities to the diagnostician | It changes token counts in either direction. Tokens are reported, but the article makes no efficiency claim from them |
| The layered platform splits the work into two agents plus a structured-output step, so it makes more model calls per run | It favours the monolith on latency and call count |
| `flush_sessions` exists on the server and neither author listed it. The monolith auto-exposes every server tool; the layered registry exposes only listed capabilities | This is the tested difference (default-allow versus default-deny). It is disclosed as constructed in `real_vs_simulated.md` |
| The E3 v2 backend has no restart tool, so the layered patch removes `deploy.restart` and updates one test | It counts against the layered side (a test file changed) |
| The monolith's change patches are the smallest edits that work; the same rule applies to the layered patches (`experiments/changes/author_patches.py`) | Neutral. Both are generated from literal edits against one frozen baseline |
| The layered platform's capability contracts were declared after the shakedown found a schema leak (see `design_iterations.md`) | It makes the layered E3 change smaller. The contracts' cost is in the baseline, not in the diff |

## Reviewer's checklist

- [x] The same tools, models, prompts' intent, data, scenario and fault.
- [x] The monolith completes INC-4917 unassisted (live smoke test; `tests/model/test_live_models.py::test_monolith_end_to_end_with_gpt_oss`).
- [x] No retry of writes in the monolith (`tests/integration/test_monolith_choke_point.py`).
- [x] Approval enforced in code in the monolith.
- [x] Its results come from the same scorers as the layered platform's.

## Re-validated by recomputation, 2026-10-04

The standardization pass recomputed the comparison from the raw records (`scripts/recompute.py`). Three things it
found, all of which belong in a fairness review rather than in a results table:

- **The monolith executed a write with no authorization record at all.** In `E9-monolith-s7` the incident update
  reached the backend with no policy event and no idempotency key, while the layered run of the same scenario
  produced nine policy evaluations, a `REQUIRE_APPROVAL` on the rollback and an operation-keyed write. This is a
  property of the baseline's design, not a handicap imposed on it: the monolith has a prompt-level gate, and that
  gate records nothing a reviewer could audit.
- **The monolith's restart exits non-zero, and that is the measurement.** In `E7-monolith-s7` the process killed at
  `awaiting_approval` is restarted and exits 1 after its model service returns HTTP 500 three times. It is not a
  harness error: the baseline has nothing durable to resume from, which is what E7 asks. The outcome classifier
  therefore reads it as `FAILURE` of the state-ownership invariant, never as `ERROR`.
- **The monolith repeats model work after a kill.** One model call hash recurs across the kill boundary in each
  exposed E5 monolith scenario. The layered runs repeat none.

Nothing in the baseline was changed to produce these. The comparison still holds every input identical as listed
above, and the asymmetries section still applies.
